descriptions: self-luminous everywhere, dwelling in the heart of those who love (Kaṭuveḷi 34)
light within like the inner light of a ruby (Aḻukaṇṇi 39)
without here or there, everywhere as light, fullness of bliss, filled with grace (Tāyumāṉavar)
negations: not seen by the four Vedas (Pattirakiriyār 48)
not reached by pilgrimage or holy bathing (Kaṭuveḷi 15)
beyond elements, senses, qualities and instruments (Paṭṭiṉattār, Tiruvēkampamālai 31)
relation_to_self: Within the body and the heart; the seeker longs to stand as 'I am He' (Pattirakiriyār 219) and asks 'who am I, who are you'; guru and Lord are one; devotional and non-dual voices coexist.
relation_to_world: The world and body are real enough to be perfected (TM 724–725) yet impermanent, a bubble and a leaking pot; macrocosm and microcosm mirror each other.
caveat: The Siddhars are not one school: some speak as Śaiva devotees, some as non-dualists of the void, some as alchemists of the deathless body. They would reject any reading that places the ultimate in a temple image or makes caste or scripture a condition of reaching it.

names.name: Civam (as the source of the medical knowledge)

descriptions: Siddha medicine places itself within the Siddhars' Śaiva frame: Śiva is the first teacher of medicine; body and cosmos share the five elements and the ninety-six principles.
relation_to_self: The soul inhabits a body of 96 principles whose health is the balance of the three humours.
relation_to_world: The body is built of the five elements, like the world; macrocosm and microcosm correspond.
caveat: A medical system: it does not itself argue a doctrine of the ultimate, but borrows the Siddha/Śaiva frame; practitioners hold a range of religious views.
